title: Two Fundamental Polynomials: Characteristic vs Minimal
content: Every n×n matrix M over a field K has two associated monic polynomials. The characteristic polynomial charpoly(M) = det(λI − M) has degree exactly n and encodes the eigenvalues with multiplicity. The minimal polynomial minpoly(M) is the unique monic polynomial of smallest degree that annihilates M. The central structural fact — minpoly | charpoly — means every eigenvalue (root of charpoly) is also a root of minpoly. The gap between the two polynomials reflects the Jordan structure: a Jordan block of size k for eigenvalue λ contributes (X − λ)^k to charpoly, but only the largest such k across all Jordan blocks for λ appears in minpoly. This file proves all key relationships between the two polynomials using Mathlib's minpoly and Matrix.charpoly APIs, leveraging Cayley-Hamilton (charpoly(M)(M) = 0) and the universal property of the minimal polynomial (minpoly divides any annihilating polynomial). The companion file MinpolyCharpoly serves as a companion to CayleyHamilton.lean and cayley-hamilton-minpoly.
mathContext: For $M \in \text{Mat}_{n}(K)$: $p_M(\lambda) = \det(\lambda I - M)$, $\deg p_M = n$. Minimal polynomial $m_M$ = $\gcd$ of invariant factors of $(\lambda I - M)$. Key: $m_M \mid p_M$, $1 \leq \deg m_M \leq n$. Diagonalizable $\Leftrightarrow$ $m_M$ squarefree. Cyclic vector exists $\Leftrightarrow$ $m_M = p_M$.

title: minpoly_dvd_charpoly: The Core Divisibility Theorem
content: minpoly_dvd_charpoly proves minpoly K M | M.charpoly for any matrix M over a field K. The proof reduces to two facts: (1) Cayley-Hamilton (Matrix.aeval_self_charpoly): charpoly(M)(M) = 0, so charpoly is an annihilating polynomial; (2) the universal property of the minimal polynomial (minpoly.dvd): any polynomial annihilating M is divisible by minpoly. The integrality prerequisite — that M is integral over K — is handled by matrix_is_integral (Matrix.isIntegral). In Mathlib, minpoly is defined for any element of an algebra that is integral over the base ring; for matrices, integrality is guaranteed by Cayley-Hamilton itself. The Lean proof is a one-liner: Matrix.minpoly_dvd_charpoly M. The monic hypothesis is needed to distinguish the polynomial from the zero polynomial (which trivially divides everything).
mathContext: $\text{minpoly}(M) \mid \text{charpoly}(M)$: since $\text{charpoly}(M)(M) = 0$ and $\text{minpoly}(M)$ divides every annihilating polynomial, we get $\text{charpoly}(M) = \text{minpoly}(M) \cdot q(X)$ for some $q \in K[X]$. The quotient $q$ has $\deg q = n - \deg m_M \geq 0$.

title: Degree Bounds: deg(minpoly) ≤ n via Chained Inequalities
content: minpoly_degree_le_dim proves deg(minpoly K M) ≤ Fintype.card n by chaining two inequalities through a calc block. Step 1: minpoly_degree_le_charpoly_degree gives deg(minpoly) ≤ deg(charpoly) using Polynomial.natDegree_le_of_dvd, which requires divisibility (minpoly | charpoly) and that the divisor is nonzero — supplied by charpoly_monic.ne_zero. Step 2: Matrix.charpoly_natDegree_eq_dim gives deg(charpoly) = Fintype.card n (since det(λI - M) is a degree-n polynomial in λ). The bound deg ≤ n is the key quantitative fact: the n+1 matrices {I, M, M², ..., M^n} are linearly dependent in Mat_n(K) (which has dimension n²), so there must exist a polynomial of degree ≤ n annihilating M. The minimal polynomial has the smallest such degree.
mathContext: $\deg(m_M) \leq \deg(p_M) = n$. Chain: $\deg(m_M) \leq \deg(p_M)$ (from $m_M \mid p_M$, $p_M \neq 0$) and $\deg(p_M) = n$ (Leibniz determinant formula). The span $\{I, M, \ldots, M^n\}$ has $n+1$ elements in $\text{Mat}_n(K) \cong K^{n^2}$, so they are linearly dependent for any $n \geq 1$.

title: Annihilation, Universal Property, and Monicness
content: Parts 4–5 characterize the annihilation behavior. charpoly_annihilates (Matrix.aeval_self_charpoly): M satisfies its characteristic polynomial — Cayley-Hamilton, here used as a Mathlib lemma rather than proved from scratch. minpoly_annihilates (minpoly.aeval): M satisfies its minimal polynomial — the defining property of minpoly. minpoly_divides_annihilator: if p(M) = 0 then minpoly | p — the universal property of minpoly as a generator of the annihilator ideal. both_monic bundles minpoly.monic and charpoly_monic: both polynomials are monic, which is essential for the well-posedness of polynomial division and for proving divisibility results (monic polynomials are nonzero). The universal property (minpoly_divides_annihilator = minpoly.dvd) makes the minimal polynomial the 'canonical' annihilating polynomial: not just the smallest by degree, but the one dividing all others — the generator of the entire annihilator ideal.
mathContext: The annihilator ideal $\text{Ann}(M) = \{p \in K[X] \mid p(M) = 0\}$ is principal: $\text{Ann}(M) = (m_M)$. So $p(M) = 0 \Leftrightarrow m_M \mid p$. Both $m_M$ and $p_M$ are monic (leading coefficient 1), making the quotient $p_M / m_M \in K[X]$ a monic polynomial.

title: Root Propagation and Basis-Independence via Linear Maps
content: minpoly_root_is_charpoly_root proves: if minpoly(M)(α) = 0 then charpoly(M)(α) = 0. The proof is direct: obtain quotient q from minpoly_dvd_charpoly (charpoly = minpoly · q), then eval both sides at α and use hα : minpoly(α) = 0 to get 0·eval(q,α) = 0. The converse holds over algebraically closed fields (every eigenvalue is a root of both charpoly and minpoly by divisibility), but can fail for non-eigenvalues. Note that the comment in the file says 'vice versa over algebraically closed fields' — more precisely, over any field, the roots of charpoly (eigenvalues) are the same as the roots of minpoly, since both divide a power of the other over the splitting field. minpoly_eq_linmap_minpoly (Matrix.minpoly_toLin') proves basis-independence: the minpoly of matrix M equals the minpoly of the corresponding linear map M represents. This shows the minimal polynomial is an intrinsic invariant of the linear transformation, not dependent on basis choice.
mathContext: $\alpha$ a root of $m_M$ $\Rightarrow$ $\alpha$ a root of $p_M$. Over $\overline{K}$: roots of $m_M$ = roots of $p_M$ = eigenvalues of $M$. Basis-independence: if $\phi = M \circ \text{basis}$, then $m_M(M) = 0 \Leftrightarrow m_M(\phi) = 0$, confirming $m_M = m_\phi$.

title: Extremal Examples: Identity (degree gap n−1) and Zero Matrix
content: Parts 8–9 verify the theory on the simplest matrices, which happen to be the extremal cases for the degree gap. For the identity matrix I_n: charpoly = (X − 1)^n (all eigenvalues = 1, each with multiplicity n) and minpoly = X − 1 (since I − I = 0, and X − 1 has degree 1). The degree gap is n − 1 — maximal, reflecting that I has only one distinct eigenvalue. For the zero matrix 0_n: charpoly = X^n (eigenvalue 0 with multiplicity n) and minpoly = X (since 0·0 = 0). Again the degree gap is n − 1. In contrast, a companion matrix C_f (the canonical matrix for a monic polynomial f of degree n) satisfies minpoly = charpoly = f — degree gap 0, the other extreme. The uniqueness theorem minpoly_dvd_annihilating_monic (= minpoly.dvd) asserts that minpoly divides any annihilating polynomial, characterizing it as the generator of the annihilator ideal.
mathContext: Identity: $m_I = X - 1$, $p_I = (X-1)^n$, gap $= n-1$. Zero: $m_0 = X$, $p_0 = X^n$, gap $= n-1$. Companion matrix $C_f$: $m_{C_f} = p_{C_f} = f$, gap $= 0$. General: $1 \leq \deg m_M \leq \deg p_M = n$.
